extracted.intended_audience: readers of humorous fiction; writers studying comic technique and observational comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for crafting comic narrative scenes (character-driven mishaps, social satire, physical comedy, and irony) in the vein of late-19th/early-20th observational humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boating-costume practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: “A ‘boating costume,’ it would be as well if all ladies would understand, ought to be a costume that can be worn in a boat, and not merely under a glass-case.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate, realistic props and clothing for the scene: comic friction arises when characters wear impractical, overly-staged outfits (the French fashion-plate costumes) in a context that demands practicality. The passage gives the example of women dressed for a photographic studio who are ruined by ordinary picnic/boat conditions (splashing, dusty grass, leaning on tree-trunks). This mismatch between costume and context is an exploitable source of comedy and social commentary; anti-pattern is dressing characters as if for display rather than for action, which 'uttersly spoils an excursion'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character contrast: preoccupation with appearance spoils events
rubrics_metrics.description: “It utterly spoils an excursion if you have folk in the boat who are thinking all the time a good deal more of their dress than of the trip.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create comedic tension by placing characters whose priorities clash with the situation (beauty/vanity vs. rustic adventure). Show their discomfort (shrinking at spray, guarding dresses) and the effect this has on other characters (narrator's irritation, altered behavior). This yields situational comedy and allows other characters to be caricatured (over-delicate, faint-hearted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalating repetition and absurd circularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative of the maze: repeated attempts to escape lead them back to the centre again and again; 'Whatever way they turned brought them back to the middle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cycles and repetition that escalate in absurdity (turn, consult map, think they're progressing, find themselves back at center). Repetition with small variations compounds the comic effect and breeds desperation in the characters and exasperation in the reader. Allow the crowd to become habituated to the absurdity (some stop and wait), which heightens the irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overconfident but incompetent leader as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Harris studies a map, declares the maze simple, leads a procession of people who trust him—only to discover the map is misleading and he doesn't know where they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy a character who projects confidence and expertise but is actually mistaken: their certainty draws followers and creates responsibility for the escalating farce. The leader's attempts to save face (pretending the centre was intended) generate further comedic complications. Use the leader's explanations and rationalizations for humor (e.g., insisting the map is right if they knew where they were).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry of incompetence (authority figures fail too)
rubrics_metrics.description: The young keeper who is supposed to help also gets lost; 'when he got in, he couldn’t find them, and he wandered about, trying to get to them, and then he got lost.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mirror the protagonists' incompetence in supposed authorities to deepen the absurdity and remove an easy escape route. When helpers fail (keeper also lost), the situation becomes more hopeless and funnier. This symmetry undercuts expectations about rescue and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sudden intrusion to deflate sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator's idyllic reverie is broken by a shrill piping voice and an officious old man: the narrator's noble thoughts are interrupted by comic bluntness about tombs and skulls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a lofty, sentimental tone and then abruptly introduce a mundane or crude intrusion to produce comic deflation. The clash between elevated introspection and officious interruption creates irony and laughter (e.g., the sexton's insistence on showing tombs and skulls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical slapstick and mishap for immediate comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Harris leaning over to fetch a bottle and ending up head-first in the hamper with his legs sticking up; the boat striking the bank when he pulls the wrong line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-timed physical mishaps and vivid, visual description to create immediate, robust comedy. Build up to the pratfall with fumbling actions (reaching deeper, steering poorly), then deliver the physical image. Physical comedy works best when consequences affect social dynamics (embarrassment, anger, altered plans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amateur performer’s misremembered routine as comic anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended depiction of Harris's comic singing showing failures: forgetting lines ('never remember more than the first three lines'), mixing up songs, bad timing, odd vocalization, and false confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray over-eager performers who imagine themselves talented but repeatedly fail at basic elements (lyrics, timing, pitch). The passage lists specific failings audiences tolerate in comic songs, but then shows the worse anti-patterns: only knowing three lines, repeating them, breaking off to snigger, improvising, confusing songs—all of which amplify embarrassment and create social comedy. Use the audience’s expectations (words, chorus) as a foil for the performer’s incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obliviousness / self-deception for character comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Harris 'never sees what an ass he is making of himself' and honestly believes he has given a treat; he wants to sing again after dinner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters blissfully unaware of their own failings; their self-deception produces dramatic irony as readers and other characters perceive the absurdity. This sustained lack of self-awareness can be a recurring source of laughter, especially when the character persists despite repeated corrective feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social contagion and mimicry of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator admits: 'When they tittered, I tittered; when they roared, I roared; and I also threw in a little snigger ... I considered this particularly artful.' Audience laughter is shown to follow leaders (the two young men) and escalate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit how groups take emotional cues from a few instigators: depict a couple of characters signaling amusement and show how the rest follow, sometimes without understanding why. This can itself be satirized (laughing at cues, not content) to critique social performativity and to create layers of humor (contagious laughter leading to mass mirth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony by misinterpretation (tragedy mistaken for comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Herr Slossenn Boschen sings a genuinely sad German song, but the assembled English audience (following the two students' cues) laughs and interprets it as comic; the professor is outraged—'It appeared that the song was not a comic song at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tone–content mismatch and cross-cultural misunderstanding to produce irony: present a solemn or tragic performance and show how audience cues or cultural differences reframe it as comic. The resulting outrage or hurt from the original performer can then fuel further comedy (the crowd's hysteria vs. the performer’s indignation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose pretension by contrast with outsiders
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'fashionable and highly cultured party' is undone (or given perspective) by two 'commonplace' young men who introduce a comic element that the group fails to understand correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast a pretentious, highbrow milieu with plain, disruptive outsiders to satirize social affectation. Let the outsiders’ behavior reveal the vanity and artificiality of the hosts (their imitation of laughter, their misplaced pride). This social-contrast technique highlights hypocrisy and produces comedic critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste-based caricature: comic judgments about color and dress
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator critiques Harris’s taste: 'Harris always keeps to shades or mixtures of orange or yellow ... His complexion is too dark for yellows. Yellows don’t suit him.' George's blazer is called 'loud' and compared to an object to frighten birds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exaggerated, opinionated commentary on fashion and taste to produce character-based comedy. Caustic comparisons and hyperbolic judgments about color, style, and appropriateness reveal personality and create comic friction among friends. Such judgments can also set up future misunderstandings (fear of attracting attention to the boat).
